title: Canonical derived specialization, fibre and cospecialization arrows
statement: For a scheme $S$ [def-pc-scheme], an abelian etale sheaf $F$ [def-weil-pbc-abelian-etale-sheaves], geometric points $s:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$ and $t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega'\to S_{(s)}$ [def-weil-geometric-point], define derived stalks by the exact geometric stalk functor [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks] on bounded below derived categories [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories]. The canonical specialization [def-weil-pbc-etale-stalk-specialization] is natural in $F$; define its bounded below derived transformation by applying it termwise, equivalently by deriving the natural transformation and conjugating by the exact-functor comparison isomorphisms. For a geometric-point cartesian square with horizontal maps $k:Z\to X$, $s:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$ and vertical maps $q:Z\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, $f:X\to S$, define the fibre map $(Rf_*K)_s\to R\Gamma(Z,k^{-1}K)$ as derived exchange [def-weil-pbc-derived-exchange] followed by global sections and Leray [lem-weil-pbc-cohomology-pullback-derived-unit]. Here inverse image and direct image are [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image], [def-weil-pbc-derived-inverse-image], [def-weil-pbc-direct-image], the derived adjunction is [prop-weil-pbc-derived-inverse-image-adjunction], and derived global sections are [def-weil-pbc-etale-cohomology]. Explicitly, use the inverse-image stalk isomorphism [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-pullback-stalk], apply the identity-point stalk to derived exchange, and invert the canonical derived global germ [def-weil-pbc-derived-global-germ] for $q$; the identity-point germ is invertible over an algebraically closed field. This recipe is also defined for any commutative geometric-point square. For the strict henselization $S_{(s)}$ [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], put $X'=X\times_S S_{(s)}$, with projections $p:X'\to X$, $f':X'\to S_{(s)}$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. For $u:\operatorname{Spec}\Xi\to S_{(s)}$, the outer-square fibre map is followed by the canonical inverse-image composition comparison to $R\Gamma(X_u,u_X^{-1}p^{-1}K)$. For $K=G[0]$, use the canonical degree-zero comparison so that the coefficient is $u_X^{-1}((p^{-1}G)[0])$. At the distinguished closed lift $c$ of $s$, transport the source along $cg=s$ from [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-functoriality](1). Finally, for $f$ locally acyclic relative to $G$ [def-weil-pbc-local-acyclicity-abelian-sheaf], write $i:X_c\to X'$, $h:X_t\to X'$, $K'=(p^{-1}G)[0]$ and $\beta:K'\to Rh_*h^{-1}K'$ for the derived unit. Define cospecialization by inverse Leray for $h$, then restriction along $i$ (derived unit followed by Leray), then $R\Gamma(X_c,(i^{-1}\beta)^{-1})$. The inverse exists by [lem-weil-pbc-local-acyclicity-closed-fibre-unit]. No quasi-compactness, properness or torsion hypothesis is needed to define these arrows. No algebraicity restriction is placed on $t$.
